intro.title: Insert coin
text: You, {{name}}, step into a forgotten arcade. Pixel Rome flashes on a cabinet. A river of light pulls you into a pixel city.

Luma the lantern owl lands beside you. "The Glitch Gremlins stole our city light. Twelve friends hide among the landmarks. Find the real ones, learn their stories, and collect at least seven before you challenge Bolt-Bot."

You start with 10 hearts, 4 tokens and 60 Pixel Power. Each move costs 1 power. Each new friend adds 2. Food fills hearts; drinks raise your heart limit. Watch for costume zips, green eyes and engine oil. Never spend your last token!
Western zodiac signs are a cultural tradition, not scientific predictions. They are not the same as the modern astronomical constellations.

This expanded adventure has 161 story sections and 16 backpack items, the same count as Hong Kong. Explore the station, arcade, market, courtyard and hidden vault. Finish the Explorer notebook and balance lesson before approaching the beacon. Each route is a branch; you will not visit every ending in one run.

hub.title: Rome after dark
text: Six stops, twelve friends. Pick your own route. All twelve is the explorer challenge! This fictional map is not walking directions.

The beacon stays closed until you earn the Explorer stamp at the city discovery desk and finish balance training in the courtyard. Both quests give a one-time power boost. Optional tools, food, transit and hidden paths can make your longer route safer.

transit.title: Via delle Lanterne
text: A sleepy station is tucked between Colosseum and the glowing city map. Its signs point into a fictional transport network made for this game. Luma taps the timetable with one wing. "We are exploring stories, not following real directions. Never use this map to plan a journey."

Behind the counter, a little owl is trying to fold a map wider than its wings. A shiny machine offers an Explorer Pass, while a hurried crowd follows a sign that reads FASTEST WAY EVER. There is no price in real money. Your arcade tokens and Pixel Power are the only stakes.
You can help first, study the platform, or walk down to the river. The station pass will let you choose the safer story route without another token.

station_owl.title: A map with too many folds
text: The owl grips one corner, but every time it folds the map, another corner springs open. You could laugh and hurry away. Instead, look at the drawing: six landmark pictures, one little compass and a blank space for a name. "I tried to remember everything at once," the owl sighs. "Could you help me find just the next step?"

Luma suggests starting with one landmark you recognise. The lesson is part of the story: break a large problem into smaller steps. A polite choice earns a useful pass and a feather. Ignoring the owl leaves the transport problem unsolved.

choices.label: Fold one panel at a time

station_help.title: One fold at a time
text: You point to Colosseum and fold away the other panels. The owl tries again. This time the map closes neatly. "A small clear step beats a huge muddle," it says, stamping a Pixel Explorer Pass for you.

The pass belongs only to this fictional arcade city. It is not a real transit card and makes no claim about fares or access. You also receive a silver feather and a one-time burst of eight power. Helping again will not produce more rewards. The owl waves you toward the platform.

station_ignore.title: The rushed goodbye
text: You stride away before the owl finishes speaking. The map pops open again, covering its spectacles. Nobody is hurt, but you leave without the Explorer Pass. Luma glances back. "We can still choose kindness next time. A mistake does not have to become a habit."

The platform remains open. Without the pass, its safe route costs a token. You can return to help, walk back to the city map, or keep exploring another route. A hurried decision closes a convenience, not the whole adventure.

platform.title: Mind the pixel gap
text: Two doors slide open. The first is marked WAIT FOR SPACE. The second flashes JUMP NOW. Tiny arrow stickers peel off the floor and reveal gremlin eyes beneath them. "If a shortcut asks you to take a silly risk, it is not a shortcut," Luma says.

This is an imaginary platform, but the choice is clear. The safe car takes you to the next landmark. Crowding into the flashing car costs hearts, while following an unmarked car lands you at a depot. The game never rewards stepping into a track area. Your Explorer Pass covers the safe ride.

choices.label: Pay 1 token for the safe train

train_safe.title: A seat beside the window
text: You wait until the doors are clear. Inside, a tiny fox makes space for the owl and points to the line of landmark pictures above the window. Buildings drift past in bands of purple, gold and teal. There is time to notice a fountain, a bridge and a row of shop awnings instead of racing past them.

The safe route ends at the next story stop. It gives no real timetable, fare or route information. Luma draws a little star beside the station in your map. You protected your hearts by waiting. Your patience is useful even when it earns no extra item.

choices.label: Step out at the next landmark

train_rush.title: The squashed carriage
text: You dash into the flashing car. It is full of gremlin luggage, each suitcase bigger inside than outside. A springy hatbox bounces into your shoulder and a stack of rubber boots lands on your foot. BOP! Two hearts disappear.

Luma steers you back onto the safe side of the doors. "There is always another story route. We do not need to push." The car deposits you at the landmark anyway, but this was an expensive way to save no time. The trap happens only once; its gremlins run out of hatboxes.

wrong_train.title: The quiet depot
text: The unmarked carriage rolls into a room full of sleeping pixel trains. A maintenance cat peers over a toolbox. "Visitors use the signed platform," it says. "This is the end of the line, not a secret shortcut."

You have lost a few squares of Pixel Power wandering here. Nobody needs to climb a fence or enter a real maintenance area. The cat opens a perfectly ordinary return door. You can thank it, return to the map and read the station signs more carefully next time. A wrong turn is recoverable.

river_pier.title: Tiber story pier
text: A toy boat bobs beside the water. The city scenery is inspired by Rome, but this ferry is an invented story route. A captain in a blue cap counts life rings while a gremlin in a fake moustache whispers, "No need to wait for boarding. Leap across!"

Luma points at a sign: WALK, WAIT, LISTEN. You can board the safe boat with your Explorer Pass, pay one arcade token, or listen to the captain first. A leap is a dice test that can cost hearts. It is a fantasy trap, never advice for a real waterfront.

river_captain.title: Tea in the wheelhouse
text: The captain sets a warm cup on the desk and asks what you noticed today. You tell a story about a real friend, not a disguised gremlin. "Good observation makes good company," the captain replies. A little wooden whistle rests beside the cup.

The whistle can distract Bolt-Bot before your duel. This is a one-time gift, not an endless source of equipment. The captain also restores a little lost power. You can now board safely with a pass the captain lends you, or return to the map without taking the boat.

river_ride.title: Across the painted water
text: The captain waits until everyone is seated. The toy ferry crosses a ribbon of water with broken moonlight on its surface. Luma watches the reflections turn ordinary windows into little golden ladders. A passenger hums a tune; another sketches the skyline.

You are not collecting every clue on this ride. Some moments are for looking. At the next landing, the captain points to the landmark and wishes you a careful journey. The imagined boat connects story chapters, not actual ferry services. Your pass stays in the backpack for another fictional ride.

river_splash.title: The wobbly gangplank
text: The gremlin lifts its fake moustache and laughs. You stop before the leap, but the toy gangplank still tilts and splashes your shoes. A captain throws a towel, not a challenge. "Safe boarding wins," Luma says.

Two hearts are lost to the fantasy splash. You can return to the pier and choose a safer option. There is no hidden reward for repeating it, and the captain will not let anyone try the leap again. The river scene is illustrated fiction; stay behind real waterfront barriers.

arcade.title: The pocket arcade
text: A row of small machines hums behind a striped curtain. One contains a brass key. Another offers a race against a clockwork beetle. Every prize is imaginary and every stake is an arcade token. Luma reads the rule panel aloud: "Two dice. Eight or more wins. Seven halves Luck. Below seven costs two Luck."

The key opens a story vault; the race pays game tokens. The machines are optional. You can take the safe road and finish without winning a gamble. Never spend the last token. These chances are visible so a player can decide rather than mistake a flashing light for a promise.

claw_test.title: The wobbling claw
text: The rule lights flash one by one. The machine will roll two dice and show the result before you continue. A win is eight or more. Exactly seven is the awkward middle result and halves your Luck. A smaller result costs two Luck. The token you paid is already in the machine.

Luma folds its wings. "A fair rule can still lead to a loss. We can choose whether the prize is worth the risk." This game uses chance, not a claim about real claw machines or races. You will never need to pay real money.

seven.text: A spring bops your Luck in half.

race_test.title: The beetle sprint
text: The rule lights flash one by one. The machine will roll two dice and show the result before you continue. A win is eight or more. Exactly seven is the awkward middle result and halves your Luck. A smaller result costs two Luck. The token you paid is already in the machine.

Luma folds its wings. "A fair rule can still lead to a loss. We can choose whether the prize is worth the risk." This game uses chance, not a claim about real claw machines or races. You will never need to pay real money.

seven.text: A spring bops your Luck in half.

claw_win.title: The key drops
text: The claw closes around the key and, for once, does not wobble open. A brass glint falls into the tray. Luma checks the teeth: a moon, a star and a tiny square. They match the locked lost-and-found door you may meet later.

A key opens an option, not a requirement. You can also earn one by solving the keeper's riddle. The machine cannot give you a second key or repeat its reward. Slip it into the backpack and decide whether to explore the hidden tunnel or return to the landmarks.

race_win.title: Winner by a pixel
text: You run beside the beetle as its little wheels click against the floor. At the finish, your shadow touches the line one square first. The beetle bows and presents three tokens with a horseshoe-shaped charm. It is a friendly contest inside a fantasy arcade, not betting on a real animal.

The prize keeper marks the race as finished. You cannot farm tokens by racing forever. Luma reminds you that a lucky win does not make the next roll predictable. Save at least one token for the way home, and keep the charm for the final duel.

arcade_lose.title: A prize that stayed put
text: The machine plays a tiny sad tune. Its prize remains behind the glass, and the rule panel explains the Luck change. Luma does not pretend the loss was secretly a win. "We tried an optional chance. Now we can stop."

A different route can earn the key without gambling. The keeper has a riddle desk nearby. You can also leave with the items you already have. There is no reward for chasing a loss and no real money spent. A player who keeps choosing risky machines may run out of Luck or tokens before the finale.

prize_keeper.title: The keeper's desk
text: A rabbit keeper dusts the brass key on its desk. "I like questions more than flashing machines," it says. "Tell me something you learned at Colosseum, and this spare key is yours." A picture from your city map glows on the counter.

Read the fact before answering. This is a knowledge route to the same useful item, not a second gambling prize. A mistake costs two Pixel Power and shows the answer. You can retreat to the map and return when ready. The keeper is fictional; the landmark fact has a source.

questions.question: Which fact did you discover at Colosseum?
options: An ancient Roman amphitheatre built for public spectacles.
It is a landmark in a different city.
Its magical guardian is real history.
questions.explain: An ancient Roman amphitheatre built for public spectacles.

keeper_reward.title: A thoughtful prize
text: The rabbit smiles and moves the key across the desk. "Learning opened this door," it says. The brass teeth fit a hidden vault, but there is no pressure to use them immediately. You can keep following the landmark route and return later.

The reward happens once. The keeper also lends you pixel goggles that reveal a clue on the service-tunnel wall. These are story tools, not real safety equipment. Luma writes KEY and GOGGLES on the map so you can remember why they matter instead of carrying mysterious objects without purpose.

courtyard.title: The mosaic courtyard
text: A little courtyard sits behind the busy streets. A fountain makes square ripples and a gardener stacks cushions beneath a tree. You can hear the city, but it sounds far away. Luma lands on a low branch and finally stops talking for a moment.

There are three useful stops here: a breathing lesson, a balance practice and a lantern workshop. Each offers a one-time story bonus. None is a medical claim or a promise of real luck. The purpose is to prepare your hero and learn that calm attention can be another kind of strength.

breath_lesson.title: In, then out
text: The gardener shows you a simple rhythm: breathe in as the paper leaf rises, breathe out as it falls. There is no competition and no need to hold your breath. You can stop whenever you want. Luma tries it too, puffing its feathers into a soft round ball.

The lesson takes one story move and offers a one-time power refill. It also sets the Calm flag, which gives you a safer reply when the Glitch King starts shouting. You are learning a story skill rather than a cure or treatment. Would you stay for a quiet moment or hurry on?

choices.label: Stay and follow the gentle rhythm

breath_reward.title: A steadier glow
text: You watch one paper leaf rise and fall. The scene becomes easier to read: fountain, bench, tree, path. The gardener nods. "You do not need to solve the entire adventure in one breath." Luma puts a small CALM mark in the corner of the map.

Ten Pixel Power returns once, along with one Luck up to its normal limit. You can come here again for the atmosphere, but not for an endless refill. Calm will matter when you face the noisy king. The reward is a game rule, not a health promise.

balance_lesson.title: The low stepping stones
text: A turtle teacher has arranged flat cushions in a line. "No heights, no racing, no danger," it says. "We practise one careful step at a time." A gremlin nearby waves a spring-loaded pogo stick, but the teacher puts it away.

You may try the safe cushion route or leave. It is not a test of real fitness. The story gives a small one-time shield flag for noticing your balance. That shield reduces one point of damage in the boss duel. Luma promises there is no hidden penalty for declining the exercise.

choices.label: Take careful steps over the cushions

balance_reward.title: The turtle's shield lesson
text: You step onto one cushion, pause, and then move to the next. The turtle applauds with a very slow clap. "You gave yourself time to notice." It paints a tiny shield on the corner of your Explorer Pass.

The shield is a story bonus used in the Bolt-Bot duel, not armour you can wear in the real world. Eight power returns once. The teacher will not repeat the bonus, but you can return to read the lesson. Luma suggests looking for a lantern next: a steady hero still needs to see the path.

lantern_workshop.title: Paper, light and string
text: A mouse maker cuts paper squares into a lantern shape. The lamp inside is a cool imaginary pixel light, not a flame. "Carry a clue, not a hazard," it says. A loose loop of string and a shiny feather sit on the workbench.

If you helped the station owl, the feather can decorate your lantern. If not, the maker still offers the same useful light. Kindness changes a detail without blocking the whole route. The lantern reveals the service tunnel, and a patchwork umbrella will help in a later storm chapter.

lantern_reward.title: A pocket full of light
text: You fold the paper around the cool lamp. Its windows look like little stars. The mouse tests the handle before handing it over. "It belongs in a story tunnel, not in your mouth or near water," it jokes. Luma laughs harder than the joke deserves.

Your backpack now has a lantern and five power returns once. There is no repeat reward. The light unlocks the safest branch of the secret route, where goggles and a brass key reveal more choices. You can visit the storm cupboard or return to the landmarks with your new equipment.

umbrella_cupboard.title: The returned umbrellas
text: A cupboard contains umbrellas in every colour. One is missing a button; another has a map pattern. The mouse explains that these are returned lost items waiting for their owners. You should not simply take whichever you like.

The patchwork umbrella has a label reading SPARE FOR EXPLORERS. It is the one the maker can lend you. Choosing the labelled spare gives a safe option in the fictional rain crossing. Luma notices that careful reading helped again. A bright object is not automatically yours just because you can reach it.

umbrella_reward.title: The borrowed patchwork
text: The maker signs out the spare umbrella and shows you the small loop that holds it closed. Pink, teal and yellow patches form a star when it opens. You promise to use it carefully. Luma balances beneath the edge to make sure there is room for two.

The umbrella joins your backpack once. At the storm crossing, it opens the safe waiting route. It is not an invitation to cross a real road without checking traffic. The arcade rain is a story obstacle, and the safest choice will always say what it does before you take it.

night_market.title: The market of little lights
text: Warm windows glow around a little square. A vendor has wrapped a Gricia picnic for travelers, while another keeps two food parcels on a high shelf. You already know the city's food facts from the snack stop. Here, the food becomes equipment you may carry and use later.

Each purchase costs one arcade token, not money. Keep the last token. Food fills lost hearts up to the current limit. Water only raises that limit. A strange green snack promises to double every bonus, but its wrapper smells like engine oil. Luma asks you to read the options before choosing.

picnic_pack.title: The wrapped picnic
text: The vendor folds Gricia into an imaginary travel box and marks it FOOD: +3 HEARTS. The label describes a game bonus, not nutritional or medical advice. "Use it when you have lost hearts," the vendor says. "A full heart meter cannot grow by eating more."

You can use the box from the backpack panel. It is consumed once and heals only up to the current heart limit. The vendor does not refill it for free. Carrying a snack gives you a choice later, when you must decide whether to rest before the hidden route or save it for the boss.

sweet_counter.title: Two carefully labelled parcels
text: The counter displays Carbonara and Amatriciana. A small sign gives a source for their place in this city's food story. A second sign is more practical: each parcel is a one-use game item, and each restores two lost hearts.

You may buy either, both if you have enough tokens, or neither. The game does not ask you to reveal a diet, allergy or payment detail. These are fictional choices. A sensible hero leaves with enough tokens to continue and does not assume a glowing package is better than a clearly labelled one.

sweet_pack.title: A parcel for later
text: The vendor ties your Carbonara parcel with a little paper star. The parcel is added to the backpack, not eaten automatically. That matters if your hearts are already full: you can keep the item for a later trap instead of wasting its bonus.

Use it through the backpack's labelled button. It removes one parcel and restores two hearts up to the current limit. Buying again after it is eaten will not create a new reward; this counter supplies one parcel per adventure. Luma checks that the label is still visible and suggests carrying on.

snack_pack.title: A parcel for later
text: The vendor ties your Amatriciana parcel with a little paper star. The parcel is added to the backpack, not eaten automatically. That matters if your hearts are already full: you can keep the item for a later trap instead of wasting its bonus.

Use it through the backpack's labelled button. It removes one parcel and restores two hearts up to the current limit. Buying again after it is eaten will not create a new reward; this counter supplies one parcel per adventure. Luma checks that the label is still visible and suggests carrying on.

suspicious_sample.title: The green sample
text: A gremlin in an apron holds out a snack that glows brighter than the lanterns. "No label, no questions, enormous power!" it shouts. The wrapper has a metal zip and the smell of engine oil. A normal vendor quietly places a bin beside it.

The safest option is to reject the unlabelled sample. Taking it triggers a fictional Static Sickness: one heart is lost on each of five moves until it fades or you use warm pixel tea. This is a fantasy glitch, not a claim that green food is unsafe. Judge the suspicious behaviour, not the colour.

sample_reject.title: A clear no, thank you
text: You leave the sample where it is. The apron gremlin sputters, but you do not need to argue. Luma points to the normal vendors with readable labels. "Saying no can be the whole answer." The market lights stay warm and steady.

You receive a small one-time token reward for spotting the fantasy disguise. It does not repeat. The tea keeper still welcomes you, whether or not you need a cure. You can return to the market, pack a snack or continue your landmark collection without touching the trap.

sample_glitch.title: Static between the pixels
text: The sample tastes like a broken television sounds. BZZT! Your outline breaks into little green squares. The gremlin drops its apron and scuttles behind the counter. Luma reads the rule panel: STATIC, FIVE MOVES, ONE HEART PER MOVE.

This is a fictional game status, not a real illness. Warm pixel tea clears it. You may visit the nearby keeper immediately or keep moving until the timer fades, but lost hearts will still matter. The trap can trigger only once. The warning souvenir joins your backpack so you remember which wrapper caused the problem.

choices.label: Go straight to the tea keeper

tea_keeper.title: The warm-cup keeper
text: An old rabbit offers a cup of fictional pixel tea. "This clears an arcade glitch, not a real health problem," it says before you can misunderstand. The warm cup can be carried or used from your backpack. The keeper asks you to promise not to chase unlabeled samples again.

The tea and a water bottle are free once in this story. Tea removes Static Sickness. Water raises maximum hearts by two without filling them. Reading those two labels prevents a common mistake: a larger heart container is not the same as a healed heart. You can pack the items or leave.

tea_reward.title: Two different kinds of help
text: The keeper puts a cup and bottle in separate pockets. TEA: CLEAR STATIC. WATER: +2 HEART CAPACITY. You repeat the difference aloud so Luma knows you understood. No token changes hands and no real beverage is ordered.

Use either item with its backpack button. The tea is consumed even when there is no static, so do not press it just to see what happens. The water bonus happens once. The keeper's one-time supply cannot be collected again, and the cupboard stays closed after this visit.

rain_crossing.title: The storm crossing
text: Rain turns the pixel street into stripes of teal and violet. A crossing signal has three panels: WAIT, CHECK, WALK. A gremlin offers to sell a shortcut through an imaginary puddle, while a courier has dropped a bag of letters behind the safe barrier.

This chapter is a fantasy street scene, not a real traffic guide. The safe route is to wait at the signal. Your umbrella makes waiting comfortable. You may help the courier, inspect the suspicious sale or choose a risky game shortcut that costs power. Luma stays beside the barrier.

rain_wait.title: Under the patchwork star
text: The umbrella opens into a little star over you and Luma. You wait behind the barrier as the crossing panels change. There is enough time to notice the courier's letters and the fake sale sticker peeling off a wall. A careful pause reveals more than a sprint.

The story gives you a one-time six-power recovery. You did not earn it by taking a traffic risk. The crossing carries you to the next landmark when the signal says so, or you may stop to help the courier first. The umbrella stays in your backpack as borrowed equipment.

rain_shelter.title: The dry shelter
text: You step into the marked shelter instead of running through the storm. A station cat has set a bench there for anyone who needs to wait. Luma shakes its feathers and studies the crossing panel. There is no penalty for lacking an umbrella when a safe shelter is available.

When the signal changes, you may continue to the landmark or help the courier from the safe side of the barrier. The shelter does not grant the umbrella's power bonus, but it protects your hearts. You can return to borrow the umbrella later if you want to see that branch of the story.

courier.title: Letters in the rain
text: The courier has dropped three letters into a dry box beside the shelter. Their stamps show a moon, a lantern and a bridge. "I can read the stamps," the courier says, "but my hands are full. Could you sort them by picture while I close the bag?"

Nothing asks you to read private letters. You help using only the pictures on their envelopes. Luma is pleased that a useful task can respect privacy. Sorting the stamps earns a one-time power bonus and a thank-you ribbon for your map. You can decline without losing hearts or a friend.

choices.label: Let the courier handle the letters

courier_help.title: Moon, lantern, bridge
text: You make three little piles by stamp. The courier closes the bag before the rain reaches it. "You helped without peeking," it says, handing you a ribbon printed with tiny umbrellas. The letters stay sealed and their destinations stay the courier's business.

Eight power returns once. The ribbon is a story flag rather than an inventory item. It later lets a keeper recognise your helpful choice, but it does not unlock anyone's private mail. Luma writes HELPFUL on your map and invites you to carry on to the next landmark or the market.

courier_leave.title: A polite pause
text: You explain that you need to keep moving. The courier nods and starts sorting the pictures itself. There is no insult, no shame and no secret penalty for saying you cannot help this time. Luma waits until the bag is safe before waving goodbye.

You can continue to the landmark or return later to help if the task is still open in the story. Choosing a boundary is different from making a rude remark. The game will not pretend every optional errand is mandatory; your hearts and power still need to last through the route you choose.

glitch_sale.title: Everything is 999 percent off
text: The sign flashes a number that makes no sense. A gremlin merchant promises an invisible crown, an endless snack and a door to every ending. Its receipt is blank. Luma asks one simple question: "What would we actually receive?" The merchant changes the subject.

You can walk away or follow the sales pitch into a trap. The scene is about checking a claim before giving up something valuable. No real shop, brand or discount is being described. The game stakes are two tokens, and the option tells you that cost before you choose.

choices.label: Walk away from the vague promise
Pay 2 tokens for the mystery box

sale_safe.title: The unbought mystery
text: You keep your tokens. The sale sticker curls at the corners and exposes the gremlin's metal grin. It has nothing left to promise once you ask for a clear description. Luma circles the blank receipt with a pencil. "We did not need to prove it was wonderful. We needed to know what it was."

You may return to the crossing or city map. There is no reward beyond keeping what you already had. This branch gives a quiet success rather than fireworks, because some good decisions are simply the bad choices you did not make.

puddle_trap.title: The folding shortcut
text: The painted puddle folds up like a rubber mat. A spring underneath turns the shortcut into a slow bouncing loop. By the time you reach the barrier again, three squares of power are gone and the gremlin has slipped away.

This was an arcade trap, not a real place or traffic manoeuvre. It happens once. You can take the marked safe crossing now, use the shelter or return to the city map. If you paid for the mystery box, the two tokens are not restored. A clear loss is still recoverable when you stop repeating it.

service_door.title: The aqueduct of pixels
text: Behind a row of lanterns, an owl-shaped door is almost hidden by ivy. A label says STORY SERVICE TUNNEL. It is an invented passage in the arcade world, not an invitation to enter restricted areas in a real city. Luma waits for you to read the sign.

The pocket lantern makes the safe route visible. Without it, you can inspect the dark doorway and retreat, but bumping around costs hearts. Pixel goggles reveal the next clue. A brass key opens the vault farther in. These three items turn earlier side quests into a connected secret route.

tunnel_dark.title: A door that needs light
text: You cannot see the handle clearly. A springy doorstop bops your knee before you step back. Luma holds up one wing. "We do not keep moving when we cannot see the path." The doorway closes with a soft click.

One heart is lost once. You can return to the workshop for a lantern, or ignore the secret route completely. There is no reward for pretending darkness is confidence. Real service tunnels and closed doors are not part of this game's exploration; the whole scene is fictional. The safe option will be plainly labelled when you have the right item.

tunnel_lit.title: Squares of warm light
text: The lantern turns each tile into a tiny window. You walk through a passage decorated with returned umbrellas, repaired signs and drawings from other explorers. It is less a sinister cave than a city cupboard full of unfinished kindness.

At the end, three door panels glow. One shows a lantern reflected in water, one shows a broken zip, and one shows two green mechanical eyes. The goggles make the little lines clearer. Luma asks you to choose a clue, not guess from the loudest colour. The keeper ahead is guarding lost property, not dangerous treasure.

door_panels.title: The three painted panels
text: A real keeper has drawn the lantern on the first panel, but the other two are gremlin stickers. The first panel has hand-painted uneven edges. The zip panel clicks with a motor. The green-eye panel smells of machine oil. The goggles confirm what careful reading already suggested.

You may follow the lantern clue, try the obvious machine disguise, or return to the map. The correct path does not require goggles, but the goggles let you recognise a secret bonus later. The story rewards observation rather than a memorised button position; read the labels each time.

door_trap.title: The sticker peels off
text: The zip opens and a spring-loaded gremlin head pops out. It makes a silly noise instead of a threat, but the surprise costs two hearts. Luma taps the hand-painted panel. "The clues were there. We can read them again without rushing."

The trap fires once and then its spring breaks. You are returned to the panels, where the safe clue is still available. Goggles are not a magic substitute for noticing what a label says. Use a packed snack if your hearts are low before entering the vault; food cannot raise them past the current limit.

vault_keeper.title: The lost-property keeper
text: A round little keeper sits behind a desk covered in odd socks and spare buttons. "If you have the brass key, you can help me sort the vault," it says. "If not, my riddle will show you another route." It points to a picture from your city map.

The key is a convenient shortcut earned in the arcade. The riddle is a knowledge route available to everyone. Both lead to the same vault, and neither requires real money. The keeper reminds you that returned items stay returned; only the stolen city light and clearly marked explorer supplies may be taken.

vault_question.title: The keeper's city question
text: The keeper puts a picture of Trevi Fountain on the desk. Luma encourages you to recall the sourced fact from that landmark. If you have not explored it, you can retreat and read before returning. No guess is required just because the question is on screen.

A correct answer opens the lost-property vault. A wrong answer costs two power and explains the answer before you continue. The keeper remains friendly. The point is to connect the city's real fact to a fictional story problem, not to pretend a riddle is evidence of a historical event.

questions.question: Which fact did you discover at Trevi Fountain?
options: The Trevi Fountain marks the end of the Virgo aqueduct.
It is a landmark in a different city.
Its magical guardian is real history.
questions.explain: The Trevi Fountain marks the end of the Virgo aqueduct.

lost_vault.title: The city's lost-and-found
text: The vault contains hundreds of harmless lost things: unmatched gloves, pencils, buttons, toy wheels and umbrellas waiting for owners. In the middle floats the city light pearl. It warms your hands like a tiny painted sun. The keeper checks its label: STOLEN CITY LIGHT, RETURN TO BEACON.

You can take that pearl and three explorer tokens. The one-time reward also restores twenty power for the last chapters. This is the route's largest recharge, earned by connecting earlier tools and clues. The other lost items stay where they belong. Luma notices a secret staircase behind a shelf of returned keys.

goggle_shelf.title: The explorer shelf
text: One shelf is clearly marked SPARES FOR EXPLORERS. A pair of goggles and a whistle sit there with a note from the keeper. The goggles reveal tiny pixel patterns; the whistle can distract the robot once. They are fictional tools, not real protective gear.

If you already have these items, nothing duplicates. If not, the shelf fills the missing slots. Taking a labelled spare is different from emptying a lost-property room. Luma approves the distinction and leads you toward the stairs. There is no extra token reward for opening and closing this cupboard.

choices.label: Take the labelled spares and climb

secret_stairs.title: The staircase back to moonlight
text: The stairs curl through a wall painted with six little landmark pictures. Every few steps, a lantern shows a place you explored earlier. The hidden route joins the main story instead of replacing it. You still need seven collected friends before the boss duel.

At the top, Luma adds a SECRET ROUTE mark to your map. That flag will appear in the quest journal so you can remember what you did. The pearl stays in your backpack for the ending. You can collect remaining friends now or visit the beacon forecourt when you feel ready.

discovery_desk.title: The city discovery desk
text: A small desk displays the six landmarks of Rome in a row. A cat archivist asks you to choose one detail you can explain in your own words. The desk is an imagined learning stop; the facts on the cards come from the sources linked at the real landmark encounters.

You can study a landmark, retell a story, or show a guide how to spot a fantasy gremlin. The route ends with an Explorer stamp. It is another one-time power refill and is required before the beacon chapter, so your adventure includes discovery rather than only collecting names.

landmark_card.title: One place, one detail
text: An ancient Roman amphitheatre built for public spectacles.

This sourced fact belongs to Colosseum. In the game, a fictional friend may stand beside it, but that does not mean the character lived or visited there. The cat archivist asks you to keep those two kinds of statement apart: a real landmark fact and an invented encounter.

You look again at the pixel illustration. It is a playful simplified scene, not a measured drawing or photograph. A good explorer can enjoy the picture while checking a factual claim in the linked source. You may now add your explanation to the notebook.

choices.label: Write the fact in the notebook

story_card.title: A tale is not a travel record
text: Western zodiac signs are a cultural tradition, not scientific predictions. They are not the same as the modern astronomical constellations.

The first friend on your map is Aries. Its story clue is: Rubs real curled horns against a stone arch. In this arcade adventure, that clue distinguishes the real story friend from two mechanical gremlins. It does not turn the fictional encounter into a historical visit.

The archivist likes your distinction. Folklore, fables and cultural symbols can teach without being presented as scientific predictions or verified events. The New York Sparks, in particular, are original invented characters. Your notebook will say which parts are sourced facts and which parts belong to the game.

choices.label: Write the distinction in the notebook

clue_card.title: Evidence before excitement
text: The archivist holds up three toy masks. One has cloth stitching, one has a metal costume zip and one has a little oil stain. "A loud voice can make a weak clue feel strong," it says. "Read what you can actually see."

You explain that the game's green eyes, motor clicks and engine-oil smell are recurring fantasy disguise clues. They are not a rule for judging real people or animals. A friend's clue may change shape, but its written description matters more than where the button sits. Luma adds a small magnifying glass to the notebook drawing.

choices.label: Write the clue lesson in the notebook

discovery_notebook.title: Your explorer notebook
text: You write a short note: one real landmark fact, one cultural story, and one invented game rule. The archivist reads it back without adding anything you did not say. The notebook does not ask for a real name, age, location or account. Your chosen nickname is enough.

The desk stamps your map once and returns twelve power. The Explorer stamp is a backpack item that opens the beacon forecourt. You can finish the notebook by any of its three routes; taking all of them adds reading, not repeated rewards. The cat points you toward a tiny souvenir shelf.

souvenir_shelf.title: A souvenir of looking closely
text: The shelf holds paper postcards with no price tags. Each shows one landmark beneath a pixel moon. You choose a postcard to look at, then leave it for the next explorer. Luma notices that the best souvenir today is the explanation you can now give without guessing.

This page has no hidden stat reward. It closes the discovery branch and gives you a quiet point to decide what remains: friends, tools, food or the finale. The quest journal records your stamp. The beacon forecourt requires that stamp and the balance lesson, while the secret vault remains an optional way to carry the stolen pearl yourself.

beacon_forecourt.title: The beacon forecourt
text: Above the rooftops stands an imaginary beacon made of stacked stars. It is not an actual city building or visitor attraction. Bolt-Bot patrols the steps while the Glitch King rehearses an enormous speech behind a curtain. Your friends wait at the edge, ready to cheer but not able to make your choices for you.

Luma checks the Explorer stamp and the balance lesson. You need both before entering this longer finale, plus seven friends for the robot. A packed snack may help. You can dance to distract the robot, rest at the bench, or approach the arena. These branches make preparation part of the story rather than a decorative button.

robot_dance.title: The robot's rhythm problem
text: Bolt-Bot hears your little dance beat and stops marching. Its feet know only LEFT, RIGHT, LEFT, RIGHT, so the extra clap sends it into a harmless spin. You stay well outside its path. Luma keeps the rhythm while the robot tries to count on its square fingers.

If you carry the whistle, its soft chirp distracts the robot once and adds to your duel attack. Otherwise the dance still earns a small story flag and power bonus. The robot is fictional. There is no advice here to distract a real guard or climb past a barrier. You still have to win the duel.

choices.label: Finish the dance and take a bow

robot_dance_done.title: A very square bow
text: The robot bows so deeply that its little antenna touches the floor. You applaud politely. "NEW RHYTHM STORED," it beeps. It will remember that friendly distraction when the duel starts, but it does not abandon its guard duty.

The one-time dance bonus restores four power. A whistle also provides a duel boost through the backpack equipment rules. Luma warns you not to confuse a preparation bonus with victory: seven friends, enough hearts and a careful final decision still matter. You can rest at the bench or approach the arena now.

boss_bench.title: The last quiet bench
text: A bench beside the beacon has room for you and Luma. The city sounds small from here. Before the duel, check your hearts, Luck, power and tokens. A bigger heart limit does not mean the hearts inside it are full. Use carried food if you have lost hearts.

You cannot refill everything by sitting down forever. The first rest gives six power once; later visits give only a place to read the rules. The journal shows which side quests are finished. When you are ready, the gate will explain the robot attack and your equipment boosts before the dice are rolled.

boss_rest.title: Ready is not rushed
text: You sit for a moment and count your useful items. Lantern for sight, key for a lock, food for lost hearts, whistle for a distraction. None is useful just because it glitters. Luma likes that you can explain what each tool does.

Six power returns once. You stand up when you are ready, not when the Glitch King shouts from above. The next chapter is the same required duel as the Hong Kong adventure's boss route. Losing enough hearts will end the run; fleeing costs three power and returns you to the map. Read the rules before choosing.

king_balcony.title: The Glitch King's balcony
text: Bolt-Bot folds into a harmless stool after the duel. Above it, the Glitch King wears a crown made of sticky pixels. "HURRY! PANIC! CHOOSE BEFORE YOU READ!" it shouts. Its noise is trying to make you forget all the patient choices that brought you here.

You can use the Calm lesson, shout back and lose power, or listen to its suspicious offer. The king is fictional, and you do not need to copy its behaviour. The city light can be returned with the pearl from the vault or unlocked by the final city riddle. Neither path requires accepting a crown.

king_calm.title: A quiet answer
text: You let the king finish its noisy sentence. Then you answer at an ordinary volume: "I can read first." The crown flickers because shouting no longer controls the pace. Luma stays beside your shoulder and your friends keep the walkway clear.

The Calm lesson has become useful here, not merely a checkbox. You can return the pearl if you carried it from the hidden vault, or answer a final sourced city question. The pearl route is faster, but a question route lets a hero without it finish too. There is no need to pretend either path is the only correct way to explore.

king_shout.title: Too much static
text: You shout back. The balcony amplifies every word until the air fills with little static squares. The king seems delighted: confusion is its favourite weather. Four power disappears once before Luma nudges your shoulder. "We can stop answering noise with noise."

You may read the king's offer calmly now. The loss does not repeat, and you are not forced to keep shouting. The final riddle still offers a way to save the city. If you have the pearl, the same quiet return route becomes available after rejecting the sticky crown. A mistake changes the route without making you a bad hero.

king_offer.title: The sticky crown offer
text: The king offers you its crown in exchange for forgetting the city light. The crown promises every prize, every friend and endless power, but its underside is covered in glue. Luma points at the fine print: BECOME A GREMLIN. That is not a small detail.

You may reject the crown and choose a real ending, or accept it and reach a different ending that clearly explains the consequence. Neither option is hidden behind a vague label. The best offer is not the brightest one; it is the one that matches what you actually set out to do.

choices.label: Reject the sticky crown and solve the riddle
Reject it and return the pearl

pearl_return.title: Light returned by hand
text: You place the pearl in the beacon's open frame. Its little squares line up with the city map and every dark window begins to glow again. The king's sticky crown falls apart into harmless confetti. Luma checks that the walkway is clear before your friends gather around.

This ending rewards the hidden-vault route without demanding it from everyone. The landmark riddles you answered to collect your friends still count. The pearl is consumed as it returns to the city, and the secret-route flag remains in your journal. You can continue to the victory page and see your final score.

gremlin_ending.title: A crown with a cost
text: You put on the sticky crown. It turns your hero into a small confused gremlin and shuts the beacon's window. The promised endless prizes do not appear. The game tells you plainly: this is a different ending, not saving the city.

Luma stays outside the gate and keeps the map for your next attempt. You can restart with a new hero and reject the crown, or choose another city. Every earlier lesson still makes sense: read a claim, check its cost, and keep your own goal in view. No real item, account or money is lost.

x0a.title: The painted arch
text: A glowing arch is painted on the arena wall. A tiny sign says SECRET WAY in wobbly pixels.

x0b.title: The cardboard tunnel
text: Cardboard columns line a twisty tunnel. Arrows point left, right, then left again. This is Luma's "too good to be true" feeling.
Luma the lantern owl says: "This path feels like a dead end."

x0c.title: A blank wall
text: You reach a blank wall with a sticker: NOTHING HERE. The gremlins drew the whole tunnel as a joke. You walk back with no reward.

x1a.title: The wish basin
text: A neon basin bubbles beside the fountain. A sign says WISH BIG, TOSS FAST.

x1b.title: The grabbing hand
text: Your token spins in the air. A rubber gremlin hand pops out of the water to catch it.
Luma the lantern owl says: "This could be a trap. Are you sure?"

x1c.title: Splash!
text: The basin sprays you from every side. You lose 1 heart. The trap only works once, and your token is safe in your pocket.

x2a.title: The round-roof ladder
text: A silver ladder leans against the great round roof. It goes up into a patch of flickering light.

x2b.title: Rung after rung
text: The ladder is much longer than it looked. Every ten rungs, a painted sign says ALMOST THERE.
Luma the lantern owl says: "This path feels like a dead end."

x2c.title: The painted sky
text: At the top there is only a painted sky on a flat board. There is no beacon, no door, only a note: GOOD TRY. You climb carefully back down.

x3a.title: The rolling lantern
text: A shiny lantern rolls across the square all by itself. It seems to wink at you.

x3b.title: The pigeon crossing
text: The lantern rolls over a pile of toy pigeons. Luma hoots: "Look where you step!"
Luma the lantern owl says: "This could be a trap. Are you sure?"

x3c.title: Bump!
text: You trip over a pixel pigeon and lose 1 heart. The lantern was a gremlin decoy. The pigeons are fine.

x4a.title: The free crate
text: A wooden crate says FREE SNACKS in bright letters. The lid is held shut with a bow.

x4b.title: Pull the bow
text: The bow comes loose very easily. A spring creaks inside the crate.
Luma the lantern owl says: "This could be a trap. Are you sure?"

x4c.title: Boing!
text: A spring-loaded cardboard flower pops out and bonks your nose. You lose 1 heart. The crate holds no snacks.

x5a.title: The staircase lights
text: Little lights lead up a staircase between old houses. They blink in a friendly rhythm.

x5b.title: Up and around
text: The stairs turn left, then right, then left again. The lights blink faster each time.
Luma the lantern owl says: "This path feels like a dead end."

x5c.title: The last step
text: The staircase ends at a plain wall with one last light. The light says: THE END. You tiptoe back down.

intro.title: Insert coin
text: You, {{name}}, step into a forgotten arcade. Pixel Paris flashes on a cabinet. A river of light pulls you into a pixel city.

Plume the paper sparrow lands beside you. "The Glitch Gremlins stole our city light. Twelve friends hide among the landmarks. Find the real ones, learn their stories, and collect at least seven before you challenge Bolt-Bot."

You start with 10 hearts, 4 tokens and 60 Pixel Power. Each move costs 1 power. Each new friend adds 2. Food fills hearts; drinks raise your heart limit. Watch for costume zips, green eyes and engine oil. Never spend your last token!
New game scenes inspired by older stories, not film adaptations. These characters are fictional visitors to Paris, not historical residents.

This expanded adventure has 161 story sections and 16 backpack items, the same count as Hong Kong. Explore the station, arcade, market, courtyard and hidden vault. Finish the Explorer notebook and balance lesson before approaching the beacon. Each route is a branch; you will not visit every ending in one run.

hub.title: Paris after dark
text: Six stops, twelve friends. Pick your own route. All twelve is the explorer challenge! This fictional map is not walking directions.

The beacon stays closed until you earn the Explorer stamp at the city discovery desk and finish balance training in the courtyard. Both quests give a one-time power boost. Optional tools, food, transit and hidden paths can make your longer route safer.

transit.title: The storybook Metro
text: A sleepy station is tucked between Eiffel Tower and the glowing city map. Its signs point into a fictional transport network made for this game. Plume taps the timetable with one wing. "We are exploring stories, not following real directions. Never use this map to plan a journey."

Behind the counter, a little owl is trying to fold a map wider than its wings. A shiny machine offers an Explorer Pass, while a hurried crowd follows a sign that reads FASTEST WAY EVER. There is no price in real money. Your arcade tokens and Pixel Power are the only stakes.
You can help first, study the platform, or walk down to the river. The station pass will let you choose the safer story route without another token.

station_owl.title: A map with too many folds
text: The owl grips one corner, but every time it folds the map, another corner springs open. You could laugh and hurry away. Instead, look at the drawing: six landmark pictures, one little compass and a blank space for a name. "I tried to remember everything at once," the owl sighs. "Could you help me find just the next step?"

Plume suggests starting with one landmark you recognise. The lesson is part of the story: break a large problem into smaller steps. A polite choice earns a useful pass and a feather. Ignoring the owl leaves the transport problem unsolved.

choices.label: Fold one panel at a time

station_help.title: One fold at a time
text: You point to Eiffel Tower and fold away the other panels. The owl tries again. This time the map closes neatly. "A small clear step beats a huge muddle," it says, stamping a Pixel Explorer Pass for you.

The pass belongs only to this fictional arcade city. It is not a real transit card and makes no claim about fares or access. You also receive a silver feather and a one-time burst of eight power. Helping again will not produce more rewards. The owl waves you toward the platform.

station_ignore.title: The rushed goodbye
text: You stride away before the owl finishes speaking. The map pops open again, covering its spectacles. Nobody is hurt, but you leave without the Explorer Pass. Plume glances back. "We can still choose kindness next time. A mistake does not have to become a habit."

The platform remains open. Without the pass, its safe route costs a token. You can return to help, walk back to the city map, or keep exploring another route. A hurried decision closes a convenience, not the whole adventure.

platform.title: Mind the pixel gap
text: Two doors slide open. The first is marked WAIT FOR SPACE. The second flashes JUMP NOW. Tiny arrow stickers peel off the floor and reveal gremlin eyes beneath them. "If a shortcut asks you to take a silly risk, it is not a shortcut," Plume says.

This is an imaginary platform, but the choice is clear. The safe car takes you to the next landmark. Crowding into the flashing car costs hearts, while following an unmarked car lands you at a depot. The game never rewards stepping into a track area. Your Explorer Pass covers the safe ride.

choices.label: Pay 1 token for the safe train

train_safe.title: A seat beside the window
text: You wait until the doors are clear. Inside, a tiny fox makes space for the owl and points to the line of landmark pictures above the window. Buildings drift past in bands of purple, gold and teal. There is time to notice a fountain, a bridge and a row of shop awnings instead of racing past them.

The safe route ends at the next story stop. It gives no real timetable, fare or route information. Plume draws a little star beside the station in your map. You protected your hearts by waiting. Your patience is useful even when it earns no extra item.

choices.label: Step out at the next landmark

train_rush.title: The squashed carriage
text: You dash into the flashing car. It is full of gremlin luggage, each suitcase bigger inside than outside. A springy hatbox bounces into your shoulder and a stack of rubber boots lands on your foot. BOP! Two hearts disappear.

Plume steers you back onto the safe side of the doors. "There is always another story route. We do not need to push." The car deposits you at the landmark anyway, but this was an expensive way to save no time. The trap happens only once; its gremlins run out of hatboxes.

wrong_train.title: The quiet depot
text: The unmarked carriage rolls into a room full of sleeping pixel trains. A maintenance cat peers over a toolbox. "Visitors use the signed platform," it says. "This is the end of the line, not a secret shortcut."

You have lost a few squares of Pixel Power wandering here. Nobody needs to climb a fence or enter a real maintenance area. The cat opens a perfectly ordinary return door. You can thank it, return to the map and read the station signs more carefully next time. A wrong turn is recoverable.

river_pier.title: Seine story pier
text: A toy boat bobs beside the water. The city scenery is inspired by Paris, but this ferry is an invented story route. A captain in a blue cap counts life rings while a gremlin in a fake moustache whispers, "No need to wait for boarding. Leap across!"

Plume points at a sign: WALK, WAIT, LISTEN. You can board the safe boat with your Explorer Pass, pay one arcade token, or listen to the captain first. A leap is a dice test that can cost hearts. It is a fantasy trap, never advice for a real waterfront.

river_captain.title: Tea in the wheelhouse
text: The captain sets a warm cup on the desk and asks what you noticed today. You tell a story about a real friend, not a disguised gremlin. "Good observation makes good company," the captain replies. A little wooden whistle rests beside the cup.

The whistle can distract Bolt-Bot before your duel. This is a one-time gift, not an endless source of equipment. The captain also restores a little lost power. You can now board safely with a pass the captain lends you, or return to the map without taking the boat.

river_ride.title: Across the painted water
text: The captain waits until everyone is seated. The toy ferry crosses a ribbon of water with broken moonlight on its surface. Plume watches the reflections turn ordinary windows into little golden ladders. A passenger hums a tune; another sketches the skyline.

You are not collecting every clue on this ride. Some moments are for looking. At the next landing, the captain points to the landmark and wishes you a careful journey. The imagined boat connects story chapters, not actual ferry services. Your pass stays in the backpack for another fictional ride.

river_splash.title: The wobbly gangplank
text: The gremlin lifts its fake moustache and laughs. You stop before the leap, but the toy gangplank still tilts and splashes your shoes. A captain throws a towel, not a challenge. "Safe boarding wins," Plume says.

Two hearts are lost to the fantasy splash. You can return to the pier and choose a safer option. There is no hidden reward for repeating it, and the captain will not let anyone try the leap again. The river scene is illustrated fiction; stay behind real waterfront barriers.

arcade.title: The pocket arcade
text: A row of small machines hums behind a striped curtain. One contains a brass key. Another offers a race against a clockwork beetle. Every prize is imaginary and every stake is an arcade token. Plume reads the rule panel aloud: "Two dice. Eight or more wins. Seven halves Luck. Below seven costs two Luck."

The key opens a story vault; the race pays game tokens. The machines are optional. You can take the safe road and finish without winning a gamble. Never spend the last token. These chances are visible so a player can decide rather than mistake a flashing light for a promise.

claw_test.title: The wobbling claw
text: The rule lights flash one by one. The machine will roll two dice and show the result before you continue. A win is eight or more. Exactly seven is the awkward middle result and halves your Luck. A smaller result costs two Luck. The token you paid is already in the machine.

Plume folds its wings. "A fair rule can still lead to a loss. We can choose whether the prize is worth the risk." This game uses chance, not a claim about real claw machines or races. You will never need to pay real money.
